elements.quote: However, studies assessing their effectiveness in delivering primary prevention interventions for non-communicable disease prevention and control in LMIC settings are limited,[10] though this has been proven for developed countries.[11] Further, whatever sparse results are available are mostly through observational studies and evidence from controlled trials needs to be synthesised.
elements.reason: The Background describes the current state of knowledge (CHWs effective in developed countries, cost-effective, used in NCD programs) and the key uncertainty: limited and mostly observational evidence on their effectiveness for NCD prevention in LMICs.

elements.quote: Considering this deficiency in availability of effectiveness parameters, a systematic review on effectiveness of CHW delivered primary prevention interventions for NCDs in developing countries was conducted by the authors.
elements.reason: The need for the review is explicitly explained: the deficiency in effectiveness evidence justifies conducting this systematic review, with a stated hypothesis.

elements.quote: Only four systematic reviews assessing this effectiveness in LMIC/ developing countries could be identified after review of published literature.[11-14] Considering this deficiency in availability of effectiveness parameters, a systematic review on effectiveness of CHW delivered primary prevention interventions for NCDs in developing countries was conducted
elements.reason: The manuscript identifies and cites four previous systematic reviews, but it does not explicitly explain how the current review differs from, updates, or extends those prior reviews.

elements.quote: A community health worker (CHW) delivers NCD preventive services using informational as well as behavioural approaches. Community education and interpersonal communication on lifestyle modifications is imparted with focus on primordial prevention of NCDs and screening is conducted as part of early diagnosis and management.
elements.reason: The mechanism of action of the CHW intervention (informational and behavioural approaches, education, interpersonal communication, screening) is briefly described in the Background.
No logic model or diagram showing hypothesised relationships between CHW intervention components and outcomes is reported anywhere in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: Considering this deficiency in availability of effectiveness parameters, a systematic review on effectiveness of CHW delivered primary prevention interventions for NCDs in developing countries was conducted by the authors. This was conducted following the hypothesis that for NCD control programs employing a community health worker is more likely to be successful than routine care.
elements.reason: The review's aim and hypothesis are conveyed in the Background, but there is no explicit, formally stated objective or research question using a question-formulation framework (e.g., PICO-formatted objective statement); the objective is only implicit in narrative form.

Although this is a review of intervention effects (CHW interventions vs usual care), no planned comparisons are explicitly stated using PICO or a variant in the retrieved evidence; comparisons appear only implicitly via included trial characteristics (e.g., Table 1) and methods text.

elements.quote: A research was considered eligible for inclusion if it followed a randomised controlled study design in community settings of low middle income countries with community health worker as intervention delivery person for general or high risk population for primary prevention of NCDs as compared to routine care or enhanced routine care as comparator.
elements.reason: The seven-point eligibility criteria specify study design (RCT/cRCT), setting (community settings in LMICs), population (general or high-risk), intervention (CHW-delivered), comparator, and purpose (primary prevention of NCDs).

elements.quote: Only randomised controlled trials (community based randomised controlled trial, cluster randomised trials) published in the last 15 years (2000-2015) were included in the review... without restriction to language
elements.reason: Publication year restriction (2000-2015) and no language restriction are explicitly stated; unpublished reports were also considered.
No evidence distinguishes exclusion due to outcomes not measured versus outcomes not reported; no such distinction is reported in the retrieved text.

elements.quote: Meta-analyses were carried out separately for each outcome and type of study design (RCT/ cRCT)... In case of considerable heterogeneity (I 2 > 75%) we only carried out a narrative synthesis of the results and grouped our findings by the type of outcome measured.
elements.reason: Synthesis grouping by outcome type and study design is described, and subgroups by age/sex are mentioned, but explicit linkage of synthesis groups to review objective comparisons is only partially elaborated.

elements.quote: The time period was limited to base evidence on recently conducted studies in light of recent shift in delivery of primary health care services towards NCDs in most of the developing countries.
elements.reason: A rationale for the 15-year publication restriction is explicitly provided, tied to the shift of primary health care toward NCDs after 2000.

elements.quote: Searches of published literature ... were done in the following biomedical, and general reference electronic databases, without restriction to language: PubMed (20002015); Excerpta Medica Database (EMBASE) (2000-2015); OVID (2000-2015)
elements.reason: Only coverage date ranges (2000-2015) are given; no date on which each source was last searched or consulted is reported.

elements.quote: PubMed (20002015); Excerpta Medica Database (EMBASE) (2000-2015); OVID (2000-2015) and World PLOS Health Organization (WHO) library and Cochrane library.
elements.reason: Database names and coverage dates (2000-2015) are given for PubMed, EMBASE and OVID, but no search interfaces/platforms are specified and Cochrane library and WHO library lack coverage dates.

elements.reason: Registers are named (ClinicalTrials.gov, WHO ICTRP) but no date restrictions for searching them are reported.

elements.reason: A website (Health-Evidence.org) is named, but no explicit URL or date of consultation is provided.

elements.reason: Individual authors/investigators were contacted, but no organisations or manufacturers contacted to identify studies are named.

elements.reason: The types of individuals contacted (authors or trial investigators) and purpose are described.

elements.reason: Two reviewers screened titles/abstracts and both reviewers assessed full texts, covering numbers of reviewers at each screening stage.

elements.reason: Independence of reviewers during screening is explicitly stated.

elements.quote: Disagreements during both stages were resolved by discussion or with intervention of the third reviewer (JST) who made the final decision.
elements.reason: Disagreement resolution for both screening stages is described.

elements.quote: One of the trial had 2 sites (Nigeria and China).[28] It was decided to analyse and present the results of both sites as different studies as there were important differences in population as well as demographic characteristics.
elements.reason: A decision rule for handling multiple reports/sites is described, but no general process for resolving inconsistencies among multiple reports of the same study is reported.

elements.quote: The primary outcome of review was percentage change in population with different behavioural risk factors. Additionally, mean overall changes in levels of several physical or biochemical parameters were studied as secondary outcomes.
elements.reason: Primary and secondary outcome domains are stated (behavioural risk factors; physical/biochemical parameters), but the domains are described broadly without explicit definitions of each outcome.
No time frame of measurement (e.g. follow-up duration or time points) is specified for any outcome domain in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: The outcome abstraction from the trials was not limited to the primary outcome on which the trial was based. Efforts were made to pool results for all other reported outcomes to highlight the fact that primary prevention interventions for NCDs influence several risk factors simultaneously.
elements.reason: The authors explicitly state that data abstraction sought all compatible reported outcomes, not only trial primary outcomes.

elements.quote: Studies were pooled only if the outcomes had been measured in the same way by all studies. Where the change per group was not available [26, 30], we used end-values where randomisation was successful.
elements.reason: Methods for selecting which results to collect/pool are described: homogeneity of measurement required and use of end-values when change scores unavailable.
No changes to outcome-domain inclusion or definitions from the registered PROSPERO protocol are reported in the retrieved evidence.
No changes to the processes for selecting results within outcome domains are reported in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: The primary outcome of review was percentage change in population with different behavioural risk factors.
elements.reason: A primary outcome is identified, implicitly prioritising behavioural risk factors, but no explicit rationale for this prioritisation for interpreting conclusions is provided.

elements.quote: The tool was adapted from The Cochrane Public Health Group: Data Extraction and Assessment Template to collect information on all aspects deemed necessary as per MECIR standards[23] from studies included in the review. Primarily it captured the trial's methodological approach as well as specifics regarding how effects of the intervention were assessed. elements.reason: The variables sought are listed: methodological approach, intervention effect assessment, CHW selection, training, terminology, and supervision; Table 1 and S Tables further document participant/intervention characteristics.

elements.quote: None of the included trials had unclear or missing data related to study methodology, participants' lost to follow-up, primary outcome data, or statistical parameters, however minor queries related to data or outcome were there, for which we contacted the study's primary author via email. We recorded all missing secondary outcome data in the data extraction form and in the risk of bias table.
elements.reason: The authors describe assumptions and handling of missing or unclear information: author contact via email and recording of missing secondary outcome data.

elements.quote: The tool was adapted from The Cochrane Public Health Group: Data Extraction and Assessment Template to collect information on all aspects deemed necessary as per MECIR standards[23]
elements.reason: The data extraction tool is explicitly cited (adapted from The Cochrane Public Health Group Data Extraction and Assessment Template, with reference to MECIR standards).

elements.quote: Quality Rating of Individual trials was done using Hamilton Effective Public Health Practice Project Checklist for quantitative studies.[24] ... Additionally, Cochrane risk of bias tool was used to assess risk of bias.[25]
elements.reason: Both risk-of-bias tools (EPHPP checklist and Cochrane risk of bias tool) are named.

elements.quote: For each item, a judgement of 'High risk', 'Unclear risk', or 'Low risk' was made.
elements.reason: The response scale for Cochrane tool items is given, and Fig 2 (text_15, figure_12) visually shows the assessed domains (random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding, incomplete outcome data, selective reporting, other bias, baseline imbalance), but the domains of the EPHPP checklist are not described in text.

elements.quote: The quality assessment represented as global score is included in the 'Characteristics of included studies' table. (Table 1)
elements.reason: An overall global quality score is reported (Strong/Moderate/Weak in Table 1), but the rules used to derive the overall judgement are not described.
No adaptations to the existing risk-of-bias tools are described; adaptations mentioned relate to a data extraction tool, not the risk-of-bias tools.

elements.quote: Reviewers independently dualrated study quality and applicability using established criteria. Discrepancies were resolved through a consensus process wherein all four reviewers jointly analysed and discussed each article.
elements.reason: Two reviewers independently rated quality, and consensus-based disagreement resolution among four reviewers is reported.

elements.quote: minor queries related to data or outcome were there, for which we contacted the study's primary author via email. We recorded all missing secondary outcome data in the data extraction form and in the risk of bias table.
elements.reason: The process of obtaining/confirming information from study investigators via email and recording it in the risk of bias table is described.
No automation tools for risk-of-bias assessment are mentioned anywhere in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: Binary outcomes were reported as relative risk (RR) of outcomes in the intervention group compared to the control group. For continuous outcomes, and where baseline data were available, mean difference (MD) between the change in the intervention and control groups were reported.
elements.reason: Effect measures are specified by outcome type: RR for binary outcomes and MD for continuous outcomes, confirmed by Table 3 showing RR or MD for each outcome.

No thresholds or ranges for interpreting effect sizes (e.g., small/medium/large effect conventions) with rationale are reported in the retrieved evidence; GRADE footnotes mention effect size >2 only as a downgrade note, not as interpretive thresholds.
No evidence indicates that synthesized results were re-expressed using another effect measure; all results were analyzed and presented as RR or MD directly.
The effect measures (RR, MD) are stated but no justification for choosing them is provided in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: Studies were pooled only if the outcomes had been measured in the same way by all studies. ... For interventions with multiple comparison groups, all groups that met the inclusion criteria were included in the review and meta-analyses.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes some processes for deciding which studies entered each synthesis (pooling only studies with identically measured outcomes, combining relevant experimental and control groups into single pairwise comparisons, including all groups meeting inclusion criteria), and subgroup analysis grouping into health topics per protocol (text_17). However, it does not fully describe tabulating study intervention characteristics against planned groups for each synthesis, so reporting is partial.

elements.quote: For trials which had not accounted for clustering, sample size estimates were adjusted for design effect using an 'approximation method'. elements.reason: The manuscript describes data preparation methods including design-effect adjustment of sample sizes using ICCs from the literature, conversion of outcomes to RR/MD effect estimates, use of end-values when change scores unavailable, combining multiple comparison groups into single pairwise comparisons, handling of cross-over trial data, and recording of missing data (contacting authors, excluding one trial lacking baseline data).

elements.reason: Methods describe the tables used (Table 1 characteristics of included studies, Table 2 summary of findings with GRADE) and their contents.

elements.quote: Forest plot was generated for each comparison.

elements.quote: Meta-analysis was conducted using Review Manager (Revman) version 5.2.[29]
elements.reason: Software and version (RevMan 5.2) are explicitly reported.

elements.quote: In case of considerable heterogeneity (I 2 > 75%) we only carried out a narrative synthesis of the results and grouped our findings by the type of outcome measured.
elements.reason: Alternative narrative synthesis is described when meta-analysis was not appropriate.

elements.quote: We used the random-effects model for all analyses, to incorporate any existing heterogeneity.
elements.reason: Random-effects model reported with a rationale.

elements.quote: Meta-analyses of the correct effect estimates and standard errors from cRCTs were pooled using generic inverse-variance methods in RevMan 2012.
elements.reason: Statistical pooling method (generic inverse-variance; RR/MD effect measures) is reported.

elements.quote: Heterogeneity among the studies included in meta-analysis was assessed by visual inspection of overlap of confidence intervals, and by assessing statistical heterogeneity with the Chi 2 statistic (P < 0.1). I 2 statistic was computed to quantify heterogeneity; an I 2 of 75% and above was taken as an indicator of more than desired heterogeneity.
elements.reason: Heterogeneity assessment (Chi-squared, I-squared, visual inspection, thresholds) is fully described.
Random-effects model used, but the between-study variance estimator (e.g., DerSimonian-Laird, REML) is not reported.
95% CIs are reported, but the method used to calculate confidence intervals for the random-effects summary effect is not described.

Meta-analysis was frequentist using RevMan; no Bayesian methods were used.

elements.quote: For interventions with multiple comparison groups, all groups that met the inclusion criteria were included in the review and meta-analyses.[31] If there were more than two relevant comparison groups we combined the relevant experimental and control groups to generate a single pair wise comparison.
elements.reason: Handling of multiple estimates per study (group combination to create a single pairwise comparison) is described; design-effect adjustment for clustering is also reported.

elements.quote: Heterogeneity of costing methodologies, outcomes, preclude quantitative synthesis of economic estimates.
elements.reason: The impossibility of quantitative synthesis for economic data is stated, but reasons for other planned syntheses judged inappropriate are less systematically reported beyond the general I-squared >75% rule.
